en: The Ritual for the Lotus Samādhi Repentance; The Supplementary Ritual for the Practice and Visualization of the Lotus Samādhi; The Liturgy for the Lotus Sūtra.

Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhiyi of Waguan Monastery during the Sui Dynasty, this Dharma-gate was drawn from the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra*, and the intent of various Mahāyāna sūtras, and is intended to circulate for future generations.
1. Clarifying the Method for Practicing the Lotus Repentance Rite for Seven Three-Day Periods and Exhorting Others to Practice It.
Part One: After the Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata.
In the final five hundred years, during the age of turbidity and evil,
there will be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas,
and upāsikās who recite Mahāyāna sūtras.
Those who wish to practice the Mahāyāna path,
those who have resolved to attain the Mahāyāna mind,
and those who wish to behold the physical body of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
Those who wish to see Śākyamuni Buddha, the stūpa of Prabhūtaratna, the various emanations of the Buddhas, and the Buddhas of the ten directions;
those who wish to attain purity of the six sense faculties, enter the realm of the Buddhas, and achieve unimpeded penetration—[should do so].
If one wishes to hear what is taught by all the Buddhas of the ten directions,
being able within a single thought-moment to receive and uphold it all, to penetrate and understand it without forgetting,
and to explain and expound it without obstruction;
Those who wish to become equal companions to Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and all other great bodhisattvas;

those who wish to universally manifest form-bodies within a single thought-moment, emerging from the samādhi of cessation to reach all Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions to make offerings to all Buddhas.
One wishes to be able, within a single thought-moment, to reach all Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions;
to manifest various physical forms and perform various miraculous transformations;
and to emit great radiance, preach the Dharma, and deliver all sentient beings.
Those who enter the inconceivable One Vehicle desire to destroy the four māras and purify all afflictions.
It extinguishes all obstacles and transgressions that hinder the Path,
causes one to enter the stage of right determination as a Bodhisattva in this very body,
and endows one with all the sovereign merits of the Buddhas.
First, one should dwell in a secluded place for twenty-one days,
entering single-mindedly and with diligent effort into the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.
Even if there are those whose present bodies have committed the five heinous crimes or the four grave offenses, thereby losing their status as bhikṣus;
If one wishes to attain purity and once again possess the śramaṇa’s discipline,
and to obtain the various kinds of supreme and wondrous merits described above, one should likewise,
during the period of twenty-one days, [practice as follows].
With single-minded diligence, practice the Lotus Samādhi. Why is this?
This Lotus Sūtra is the secret treasury of all Tathāgatas.
It stands supreme among all sutras,
for it practices the great straight path without hindrance.
It is like the bright jewel within the topknot of a wheel-turning monarch, which is not given away to anyone indiscriminately.
If there are those who obtain it, they will be fully provided with all kinds of rare treasures according to their every need;
the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* is likewise able to bestow upon all sentient beings the rare treasures of the Buddha-dharma.
Therefore, a bodhisattva practitioner should not begrudge their body or life,
but should practice this sutra until the end of the future;
how much more so for a period of twenty-one days?
Question: The path of the Buddha is long and far-reaching;
what benefit would there be from practicing it for only twenty-one days?
Answer: There are three kinds of benefits, which will be explained below. 2.
Clarifying the Preparatory Methods for the Practice of the Seven-Day Period. Second: There are two kinds of practice.
First, those who have newly begun their practice;
second, those who have practiced for a long time.
This method should be employed to instruct those who have newly begun their practice.
For those who have long practiced, one should rely on the "Chapter on Peaceful Conduct" (Anlehangpin).
Indeed, all methods for the practice of repentance must be preceded by the preparatory rites (pūrvaprayoga).
Why is this? If one does not first purify the body and mind before entering the place of practice,
then the aspiration for the Way will not be set forth, and one's conduct will not accord with the Dharma.
There is no response that can be invoked.
Therefore, prior to the formal repentance,
one should for a period of seven days first discipline one's own mind and cease all distracting activities.
Make offerings to the Triple Gem and adorn the site of practice (*maṇḍala*).
Purify all garments and focus the mind with single-minded mindfulness.
Reflect upon all evil karma committed from the time this present body was conceived, as well as throughout past lives.
Giving rise to profound shame and remorse, they prostrated before the Buddha to repent;
they practiced the Way, recited the sutras, sat in meditation, and engaged in contemplative practice,
making vows with single-minded devotion.
In order to purify the body and mind of right practice within samādhi so that they are free from hindrances,
and to ensure that all aspirations of the mind are successfully realized, one must also recite the various texts for repentance that follow.
To ensure that all [practices] are thoroughly mastered. 3.

The Method for Entering the Maṇḍala with Right Clarity and Practicing Single-minded Diligence for Twenty-one Days. Part Three: The Method for Entering the Maṇḍala with Right Clarity and Practicing Single-minded Diligence for Twenty-one Days. One should enter the maṇḍala on one of the six *poṣadha* days.
On this day, the messengers of the Four Heavenly Kings and other celestial benevolent deities descend to the human realm to inspect and examine good and evil.
Upon seeing those who practice virtue,
he immediately records them in the register of the virtuous and provides them with consolation and protection.
He manifests auspicious signs in order to cause the practitioner’s mind to give rise to joy and to increase their roots of goodness.
When the practitioner first wishes to enter the maṇḍala, they should settle their mind,
thinking: "From this moment until the completion of the three seven-day periods,
during that interval, I shall practice with single-minded diligence according to the Buddha’s teaching."
Why is this? If the mind entertains divergent thoughts, it becomes intermingled with various afflictions;
this is called impurity.
Because the mind is not pure,
how could it correspond with the right path of samādhi?
Therefore, one must restrain the mind and not spare even body or life.
With single-minded diligence,
he completed twenty-one days.
He asked, saying:
The mental states of sentient beings vary according to their circumstances and conditions.
How, then, can one attain single-minded diligence?
The answer is:
There are two kinds of cultivation of single-mindedness:
first, the cultivation of single-mindedness within phenomena;
second, the cultivation of single-mindedness within principle.
Regarding cultivating single-mindedness within the midst of activities:
for example, when a practitioner first enters the dharma hall, they immediately form this thought:
During the twenty-one days,
when I prostrate to the Buddha, I shall prostrate with single-minded devotion,
my mind not distracted by other objects.
Even when performing repentance, practicing the Way, reciting sutras, or sitting in meditation,
they were entirely single-minded;
amidst these practices, their minds were never distracted.
Thus, for three weeks and seven days,
this is called practicing single-minded diligence regarding phenomena.
Second is practicing single-minded diligence regarding principles.
The practitioner,
upon first entering the maṇḍala, should form this thought:
"From this time until the completion of the three seven-day periods."
In the midst of all that is done therein, one constantly illuminates and understands it for oneself.
The mind that acts and the nature of the mind are non-dual. Why is this so?
Just as when prostrating to the Buddha, the nature of mind is neither arising nor ceasing,
one should know that for all various activities performed,
the nature of mind is entirely neither arising nor ceasing.
When observing in this manner, one sees that all minds are in fact a single mind,
because the nature of the mind has been a single characteristic from the very beginning.
When the practitioner is able to thus reflect back upon the source of the mind, the successive moments of mind continue in an uninterrupted stream.
If, after completing twenty-one days, one does not perceive the signs of the mind, this is called the method of practicing single-minded diligence within the principle. 4.

Clarifying the Method for Initial Right Practice upon Entering the Ritual Hall. Regarding the fourth section, clarifying the method for initial right practice upon entering the ritual hall: when the practitioner first enters the ritual hall...
One should be fully endowed with ten dharmas:
first, purifying the site of practice;
second, purifying the body.
Third, making offerings through the three types of action;
fourth, respectfully inviting the Triple Gem;
fifth, praising the Triple Gem.
Sixth, prostrating before the Buddha;
seventh, repenting of transgressions;
eighth, performing circumambulation while walking the path.
Ninth, recite the Lotus Sūtra.
Tenth, contemplate the single reality realm.
During the three seven-day periods, the practitioner should practice day and night in six sessions.
At the beginning of entering the dharma-assembly, one should fully cultivate these ten dharmas within a single session.
Thereafter, during each of the six sessions,
one should omit the single dharma concerning the invitation of the Buddha.
Among these ten dharmas, it is clear that while the other nine are practiced without distinction,
within this set there are some that merely explain the methods of giving,
and others that instruct on how to direct the mind and form mental recollections.
There are those who recite the phrases and sentences of the text, proclaiming them with their own mouths;
the practitioner should skillfully grasp the meaning and apply it,
for it is not strictly necessary to recite these words verbatim.

1. The First Method for the Practitioner to Adorn and Purify the Site of Practice (Dharmakṣetra): The practitioner should, in a secluded and quiet place, prepare a single room and adorn it as a site of practice (dharmakṣetra).
Set up a separate place for oneself to sit,
ensuring it is partitioned from the ritual arena (maṇḍala).
Within the ritual arena, arrange a fine, high seat.
One should install a copy of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in one fascicle;
it is not strictly necessary to install images, śarīra relics, or other scriptures—
merely place the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
One should securely arrange banners, canopies, and various articles of offering.
On the day of entering the maṇḍala,
at the time of early morning, one should thoroughly sweep the ground.
Sprinkle fragrant water and smear the ground with fragrant mud.
Light various lamps of scented oil,
scatter diverse flowers and powdered incense, and burn many kinds of renowned incense.
Make offerings to the Triple Gem,
providing whatever one's own resources can afford,
with a devoted heart and sincere intent, making them as pure and magnificent as possible.
Why is this? Because the practitioner’s inner mind reveres the Triple Gem, transcending the three realms,
and now desires to invite them for offerings.
How can one harbor such a frivolous mind?
If one cannot dedicate one's own wealth and resources to make offerings to the Mahāyāna,
then one will ultimately fail to attract the worthy or move the sages, and one's grave offenses will not be extinguished.
By what means can samādhi be brought forth? Part Two:

Clarifying the Method for the Practitioner’s Purification of the Body. Regarding the method for purifying the body of the practitioner: when first entering the maṇḍala, [one should proceed as follows].
One should bathe with fragrant water and put on clean garments;
these may be the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*) or various newly dyed robes.
If these are unavailable, one should take one's own superior garment.
One should consider this as the robe for entering the maṇḍala;
thereafter, if one leaves the maṇḍala and goes to an impure place.
One should remove the pure robes and put on ordinary clothes.
When the task is completed,
one should bathe again and put back on the original pure robes.
Entering the Ritual Hall. 3.

Clarifying the Method for the Practitioner’s Cultivation of the Three Karmas as an Offering, Part Three. Clarifying the Method for the Practitioner’s Cultivation of the Three Karmas as an Offering. First, entering the ritual hall.
Upon reaching the Dharma seat, first spread out the *niṣīdana* and stand with the body upright and leaning slightly forward.
One should first cultivate thoughts of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, desiring to bring about their salvation.
Next, one should give rise to a heart of profound reverence, shame, and earnest compassion, maintaining a clear visualization of the Tathāgata.
The Three Jewels filled the void of the ten directions,
their reflections appearing within the site of enlightenment.
At that time, he held an incense burner in his hand and burned various kinds of famous incense.
Scattering various kinds of flowers as an offering to the Triple Gem, he immediately prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, reciting aloud:

"With all reverence and single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions who eternally abide; with my mind following my body and speech, I single-mindedly bow my head in worship."
Without a distracted mind, one understands this body to be like a shadow and unreal;
regarding both the one who prostrates and the object of prostration, the mind finds nothing to be apprehended.
All sentient beings...
Likewise, entering this ocean of the Dharma-realm of the Buddhas,
one pays homage to all the Buddhas of the ten directions;
having completed one prostration, next—
One should maintain proper physical deportment and personally recite these words:
"With a single mind, I pay respectful homage to the eternally abiding Dharma of the ten directions. Having performed this one prostration, [one continues].
Next, one should rectify the body and its deportment, and personally recite:
"With single-minded reverence, I pay homage to the eternally abiding Sangha of the ten directions. Having performed this single prostration, one should proceed.
As for the method of mental application:
it is no different from what was explained above regarding the worship of the Buddha. Having finished paying homage to the Triple Gem, one should immediately kneel with the right knee on the ground.
Kneeling with the right knee on the ground,
maintaining upright posture and dignified demeanor,
he single-mindedly burned incense and scattered flowers.
With body upright and mind rectified, one should next personally recite these words:
"Holding incense and flowers with solemnity, I offer them according to the Dharma.
May these clouds of incense and flowers pervade the worlds of the ten directions."
They make offerings to the Buddhas, the sutras, and the Dharma,
as well as to the assembly of Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas,
and Pratyekabuddhas, and to all celestial immortals.
Having accepted it for the purpose of performing Buddha-activities,
one should next bring forth the visualization that these incense and flowers, in every moment of thought,
pervade all Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions.
They fashioned various kinds of precious jewels to adorn the terraces and towers,
and created all manner of exquisite colors and diverse musical performances.
They offered sublime melodies in song and praise;
they prepared various kinds of exquisite incenses such as sandalwood and aloeswood,
along with diverse delicacies and medicinal decoctions.
Exquisite and supreme flavors;
various garments and necklaces;
and flowing springs, bathing pools, and supremely exquisite tactile sensations.
They manifest immeasurable, pure, true marks of various meditative concentrations and wisdoms—
supremely wondrous Dharma gates—
that completely fill the entire dharma-realm.
I take this as a Buddhist service to make offerings to all Buddhas and the Triple Gem of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
I pray that the Triple Gem will graciously accept it and also permeate all sentient beings.
Having resolved upon the bodhicitta,
one perceives oneself before each and every Buddha;
such offerings and so forth are all without distinction.
Furthermore, may all beings of the six destinies and four modes of birth enter the ocean-like dharma-realm of my offerings,
and fully comprehend such offerings as they are.
All arise from the mind and possess no inherent nature;
the mind does not grasp or cling.
Once this mindfulness has been established, [it is perfected].
Immediately prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground, he himself declares aloud: "Having completed the offerings, I pay homage to all with reverence. 4.

Clarifying the Method for the Practitioner’s Invocation of the Triple Gem. Fourth: Clarifying the Method for the Practitioner’s Invocation of the Triple Gem. Having already performed the offerings of the three karmas, the practitioner—
Next, one should again burn incense and scatter flowers.
With single-minded right mindfulness,
turn the mind of the preceding offerings to reverently invite the Triple Gem.
When requesting the Triple Gem according to the ritual, one should direct the mind correctly toward those being invited;
reciting their names aloud,
one should invite each one in accordance with the Dharma.

Without allowing the mind to be distracted or frivolous, single-mindedly invoke: "Namo Śākyamuni Buddha. One will then know that the Dharma-body is like empty space, devoid of the characteristics of coming or going.
All other Buddhas are likewise so;
according to the thoughts and recollections of the mind,
they [appear] from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
Surrounded by the great assembly, he came to the place of practice and accepted my earnest invitation and offerings.
With single-minded devotion, invite him, saying:
"Namo to the World-Honored One Many Treasures of the past," and you should immediately bring this to mind.
The Stūpa of Prabhūtaratna emerged from the earth,
manifesting its reflection within the site of enlightenment.
Accept my offerings.
With single-minded devotion, invoke: "Namo Śākyamuni and all the Buddhas of the ten directions who manifest as emanations. One should immediately bring to mind these manifested Buddhas.
May they all gather like clouds beneath the jewel trees to receive my offerings.
With single-minded devotion, invoke and pay homage to all the Buddhas within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, visualizing them immediately in your mind.
The Buddhas of the past, such as Candrasūryapradīpa;
the Buddhas of the present, such as Śubhavyūhapadmottārajñāna;
and the Buddhas of the future, such as Puṣparāja.
May they all appear before me to accept my offerings.

With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat all the eternally abiding Buddhas of the ten directions. One should immediately bring to mind the visualization that the bodies of the Buddhas of the eastern direction are the color of yellow gold.
Endowed with the primary and secondary marks of excellence, emitting great radiance,
and surrounded by a great assembly before and behind,
he came to the site of enlightenment, filling the void of space, and accepted my offerings.
The same applies to the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
With single-minded devotion, I reverently entreat:
Namo to the Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma; the contemplation of its mind is profoundly deep.
The secret treasury of the Dharma will all appear before them,
and they shall receive my offerings.
With single-minded devotion, take refuge in the Namah to all the eternally abiding Dharmas throughout the ten directions;
immediately bring to mind the thought that all the Buddhas of the ten directions and their entire treasury of Dharma are present.
May they all appear within this site of enlightenment to accept my offerings.
With single-minded devotion, I reverently entreat: Namo Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Mahāsattva; transport your thoughts and bring him to mind.
Surrounded by immeasurable bodhisattvas, he accepts my offerings.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva; one should also visualize the mind in the same manner as described previously.
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata.
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas Avalokiteśvara and Akṣayamati.
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas Avalokiteśvara and Padmaśrī.
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas Nityodyukta and Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
With single-minded devotion, we take refuge in and entreat the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas Mahāpratibhāna and Jñānakośa.
With single-minded devotion, we take refuge in and entreat the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, Śūradatta, and Kṣitigarbha.
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat the boundless asaṃkhyeya Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, such as the Superior One (Urdhvagama) from the lower direction;

with single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat all the great Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, such as Samantabhadra Bodhisattva from within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and I hold them in my heart.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, riding upon the six-tusked white elephant king,
with a body pleasing to behold by all sentient beings and accompanied by immeasurable retinues,
comes into the site of enlightenment to receive my offerings.
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat Śāriputra and all the great assembly of śrāvakas within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat the eternally abiding Saṃgha of the ten directions, visualizing them with my mind.
All the great Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas from the ten directions emit great radiance and,
surrounded by their vast retinues,
come to this site of enlightenment to receive my offerings.
With single-minded devotion, I invoke all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Having thus completed the first round of universal invitation for all the dark deities and empty spirits, each together with their retinues,
one should immediately prostrate oneself with the five limbs touching the ground.
Then, kneeling again with the right knee on the ground, one should burn incense and scatter flowers.
Recite the names in their proper order and invoke them;
having thus invoked them three times,
one should then personally proclaim as follows:
I only pray that our original teacher, Śākyamuni Bhagavān, the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, and all the Buddhas who are his emanations,
out of great kindness and great compassion,
will accept my invitation and come to this site of enlightenment.
Out of compassion and protection for the True and Pure Dharma-gate of the Mahāyāna Lotus Sutra,
please accept my invitation and come to this place of practice.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, and the Bodhisattvas from the lower regions such as Uṣṇīṣa, and others.
May Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and all the other great Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*,
endowed with great kindness and great compassion, accept my invitation.
Having arrived at the site of enlightenment,
Śāriputra and all the great śrāvakas have all compassionately accepted my invitation.
Having arrived at this site of practice,
may all the Triple Gem of the ten directions look upon us with compassion and provide protection;
having accepted my invitation, may you come to this site of practice.
May all the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings give rise to compassion;
having accepted my invitation, may they come to this place of practice.
May all these holy assemblies graciously bear witness.
Today, for the sake of all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions,
I wish to practice the unsurpassed Bodhi of the Mahāyāna and destroy all heavy sins that obstruct the path.
I vow to attain the Lotus Samādhi and universally manifest form-bodies;
in a single thought-moment, to make offerings to all the Triple Gem throughout the ten directions;
and in a single thought-moment, to universally deliver all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions.
In order to cause others to enter the great wisdom of the equality of the One Vehicle,
he practiced with single-minded diligence for twenty-one days,
cultivating according to what is taught in the sutras.
By the power of the original vows of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the Great Master Samantabhadra, may they accept my repentance;
may it cause all that I practice to definitively shatter all karmic obstacles of transgression.
The Dharma-gate manifests as described in the sūtras; the practitioner should personally expound it through the power of their own wisdom, requesting the Buddha to perform his work.

5. Clarifying the Method for Praising the Triple Gem, Part Five: Clarifying the Method for Praising the Triple Gem. Once the practitioner has made offerings and requests to the Triple Gem, [they should proceed as follows].
One should immediately prostrate oneself with the five limbs touching the ground,
then stand upright with body aligned and dignified demeanor, focusing the mind single-mindedly,
facing the Dharma seat while burning incense and scattering flowers.
I mindfully contemplate the subtle and wondrous merits of the Triple Gem.
Your countenance is most marvelous and sublime; your radiance illuminates the ten directions.
I have previously made offerings to you, and now I come once more to behold you in person.
To the Holy Lord, King among Gods, with a voice like the kalaviṅka bird,
who compassionately pities all sentient beings— we now pay homage and,
by means of this praise of the Buddha’s merits, cultivate the unsurpassed roots of goodness of the Mahāyāna.
I respectfully offer blessings to the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of supernatural beings in the upper realms;
to Mahābrahmā and the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens;
and to Yama, the five paths of rebirth, the six fast days, and the Eight Kings.
The various kings of pestilence spirits, each with their retinues;
the deities of this land who protect the True Dharma within monasteries;
and furthermore, for the kings, sovereigns, and the myriad people of the realm.
To one's preceptors and teachers, parents, virtuous and non-virtuous spiritual friends,
temple patrons, and the faithful offerings of the ten directions;
extending widely to all sentient beings throughout the Dharma realm.
By means of these roots of goodness,
may we equally cultivate the two kinds of adornments— merit and wisdom—
and together enter the path of unarisen omniscience, thereby attaining full realization.
The actions of body, speech, and mind fill the Dharma-realm;
they praise the Triple Gem as being without birth, without cessation, and without intrinsic nature.
6. Clarifying the Method for Paying Homage to the Buddha, Part Six. Having completed the eulogies, the practitioner should, with single-mindedness, maintain upright posture and dignified deportment.
Prostrate to the Buddhas in succession.
Regarding the method of prostrating to the Buddhas, one should, in accordance with the Buddha being venerated,
mindfully recollect with a sincere heart that this Buddha’s Dharma-body is like empty space.
They manifest forms in accordance with sentient beings as if facing them before their eyes,
receiving my prostrations;
each and every other Buddha is likewise so.
One must apply the mind without allowing it to become distracted.
Furthermore, when the practitioner prostrates to the Buddha:
He knows for himself that his body and mind are empty and quiescent,
devoid of any characteristics of ritual salutation;
he also knows this body [to be thus].
Although it is unreal like a magical illusion, it is not without manifestation;
before each and every Buddha within the Dharma-realm,
this body is fully present.
Prostrate with head and face touching the ground.
The method for prostrating to the Buddha during the six periods of the twenty-one days is as follows, without deviation:
with a single-minded and reverent heart, pay homage to our Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the past Buddha Prabhūtaratna.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the emanated Śākyamuni Buddhas of the ten directions.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Buddha Kuśala of the eastern direction and to all Buddhas throughout the entire dharma-realm of the east.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Buddha Aśoka-guṇa of the southeastern direction and to all Buddhas throughout the entire dharma-realm of the southeast.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Buddha Candana-guṇa of the southern direction and to all Buddhas throughout the entire dharma-realm of the south.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Buddha Ratnadatta of the southwest, and to all Buddhas throughout the entire dharma-realm of the southwest.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Buddha Amitābha of the west, and to all Buddhas throughout the entire dharma-realm of the west.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Buddha Flower Virtue in the northwest.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to all Buddhas throughout the entire dharma-realm of the northwest.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Buddha Sign Virtue in the north.
All Buddhas throughout the entire dharma-realm of the north,
with one mind, pay respectful homage to the Buddhas who practice the three vehicles in the northeast.
All Buddhas throughout the entire dharma-realm of the northeast.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Buddha Universal Radiance of All Virtues in the upper direction,
and to all Buddhas throughout the entirety of the upper dharma-realm.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Buddha of Luminous Virtue in the lower direction.
I pay single-minded homage to all Buddhas throughout the entire dharma-realm below,
to the Buddhas of the three periods of time— past, present, and future—
and to the Seven World-Honored Buddhas.
To the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa,
I single-mindedly pay respectful homage; and to the two hundred trillion Sun-Moon-Lamp Brightness Buddhas and the Great Pervasive Wisdom-Victory Buddha of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

What is the clear right contemplation?

What is meant by contemplating that all phenomena are empty?
The practitioner should carefully observe the deluded mind of the present moment as it follows its respective objects of perception.
Is such a mind a mind because it has a cause?
Is it a mind because it has no cause?
Or is it a mind because it both has a cause and has no cause?
Is the mind that which is neither a cause nor not a cause?
Does it exist within the three periods of time?
Does it exist internally, externally, or in between the two?
Where are the footprints of this mind, and in what location do they exist?
When sought through various causes and conditions such as these, the mind is ultimately unfindable.
The mind is like a dream or an illusion; it is not real.
It is as tranquil as space, nameless, signless, and beyond conceptual differentiation.
At that time, the practitioner does not even perceive the mind as saṃsāra;

To perform repentance in this manner is called the Great Repentance.

it is called the confession of the markless state of non-offense;

One should perform this repentance with a mind like flowing water, not abiding within any phenomena. Why is this?
All dharmas—whether sins or merits—produced by deluded thoughts and inversions arise entirely from the mind.
Apart from the mind, there are no transgressions, merits, or any phenomena whatsoever.
If one contemplates that the mind is without a mind, then transgressions and merits have no owner;
one thereby knows that the nature of transgressions and merits is empty.
Thus, all phenomena are empty.
When one contemplates in this way, one can destroy all the delusions of birth and death,
the three poisons, false imaginings, and the most heavy and evil karma.
